title: Sensex ATM Straddle: The Expected Move It Prices In Before Expiry
summary: See what move the Sensex ATM straddle priced in before the 12 Nov expiry, how to set it up on the option chain, and its payoff, breakevens and risk.
body_markdown:
A Sensex ATM straddle is the at-the-money call and put of the same strike and expiry, traded together. Its price, call premium plus put premium, is the market’s estimate of how far Sensex will move by expiry, often called the expected move. A straddle buyer profits only if Sensex settles more than that many points away from the strike.


In the worked example below, the 81,100 straddle cost 1,206.25 points at the close on 9 November 2026. That priced in a move of about 1.49% before the 12 November expiry. Sensex settled at 81,911.01, inside both breakevens, so a seller kept 395.24 points per unit before costs.

## What Is a Sensex ATM Straddle?


A straddle has two legs: one call option (CE) and one put option (PE). Both legs use the same strike price and the same expiry.


The strike closest to the current Sensex level is called[at-the-money](https://algotest.in/blog/itm-atm-otm/) , or ATM. Sensex strikes are listed 100 points apart, so the ATM strike is usually the nearest round hundred.


-


Buying both legs is a long straddle. It gains if Sensex moves far enough in either direction.


-


Selling both legs is a[short straddle](https://algotest.in/blog/short-straddle-strategy/) . It gains if Sensex stays close to the strike.


-


Sensex options trade in[lots of 20 units](https://algotest.in/blog/sensex-lot-size/) , so multiply any point value by 20 to get the amount per lot.


## How Do You Calculate the Expected Move From a Sensex Straddle?


Add the ATM call and put premiums, then use that total on both sides of the strike:


-


Straddle premium = ATM call premium + ATM put premium


-


Upper breakeven = strike + straddle premium


-


Lower breakeven = strike - straddle premium


-


Priced-in move (%) = straddle premium ÷ Sensex level × 100


At expiry, only one leg can have value. If Sensex settles above the strike, the call is worth the gap and the put expires worthless. Below the strike, the reverse happens.


So the full straddle premium applies on each side of the strike, not half of it. A 1,206-point straddle needs Sensex to settle more than 1,206 points above or below the strike, not 603. The straddle tells you how far the market expects Sensex to move, not which way.

## Worked Example: The 12 November 2026 Sensex Expiry


This example uses one completed weekly expiry. Sensex options expired on Thursday, 12 November 2026, and the snapshot is the close on Monday, 9 November.


Tuesday, 10 November was a market holiday for Diwali Balipratipada. That left only two trading sessions after the snapshot, which matters in any[Sensex expiry](https://algotest.in/blog/sensex-expiry-day/) week that includes a holiday.

#### Step 2: Add the Two Premiums


-


Straddle premium: 575.55 + 630.70 = 1,206.25 points


-


Cost of one lot: 1,206.25 × 20 = ₹24,125, before charges


-


Priced-in move: 1,206.25 ÷ 81,106.65 × 100 ≈ 1.49%


In plain words, options priced in a move of about 1,200 points over two sessions. That is a big move for two days. Sensex had rallied about 10.5% in the seven sessions to 6 November, and part of the premium likely covered the risk of a gap after the holiday.


#### Step 3: Find the Two Breakevens


-


Upper breakeven: 81,100 + 1,206.25 = 82,306.25


-


Lower breakeven: 81,100 - 1,206.25 = 79,893.75


The band between them is 2,412.50 points wide. A buyer needed Sensex to settle outside this band on 12 November. A seller needed it to settle inside.

Sensex closed at 81,911.01 on 12 November. BSE’s F&O bhavcopy lists the same figure as the[settlement price](https://algotest.in/blog/30-minute-vwap-expiry-settlement-for-options-traders/) for the expiring contracts.

After the holiday, Sensex opened at 82,248.68 on 11 November. That gap of 1,142 points stopped 57.57 points short of the upper breakeven.


-


Sensex then hit 82,520.40. The 81,100 call alone traded as high as ₹1,512 that day, more than the ₹1,206.25 paid for both legs.


-


It closed the day at 81,879.40. On expiry day it rose about 19 points above the upper breakeven, and the call touched ₹1,274.15, before Sensex settled at 81,911.01.


-


The lower breakeven at 79,893.75 was never in play. The lowest level across both sessions was 81,417.39.


Breakevens are expiry levels, not intraday triggers. A buyer who held to expiry lost money, even though Sensex crossed the upper breakeven on both days. A buyer who exited near those highs could have closed with a gain before costs.

A[long straddle](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-use-a-straddle-chart-for-intraday-options-trading) can lose at most the premium paid. Here that was 1,206.25 points, or ₹24,125 per lot, if Sensex had settled exactly at 81,100.


-


A long straddle’s profit has no fixed cap, but time decay eats into both legs in every session the move does not come.


-


A short straddle can earn at most the premium received, while its loss can keep growing on a large move in either direction.


-


Selling a straddle also blocks margin. The Payoff tab on the option chain shows an approximate margin figure for the legs you add.


-


Both sides carry gap risk across holidays and weekends, as the post-holiday open in this example showed.


The Payoff tab lists breakeven, maximum loss and margin once you sign up, and marks 1, 2 and 3 standard-deviation levels around spot. Shown here with a single call leg.


## Why Does the Time of the Snapshot Matter?


The priced-in move for one expiry changes all the time. It shrinks as expiry gets closer, because there is less time left for Sensex to move. This loss of option value is called time decay, or[theta](https://algotest.in/blog/option-greeks/) . The straddle also rises and falls with[implied volatility](https://algotest.in/blog/implied-volatility-and-how-to-read-and-compute-iv/) .

Sensex settled inside both bands. Still, the Friday straddle cost 347.40 points more for the same expiry.


That’s why every priced-in move needs a time stamp. “The straddle is 1,206” means little until you add “at Monday’s close, two sessions before expiry”.


## Straddle Price vs Expected Move


Treat the ATM straddle as the market’s estimate of a typical move, not a limit. Real moves often finish above or below it.


Some traders and tools shrink the straddle to about 85% and call that the expected move. Here, 85% of 1,206.25 is 1,025.31 points, which gives a band of about 80,081 to 82,132 around the snapshot close. Sensex settled inside that band but broke above it during the session on 11 November.


The gap between the move options price in and the move that actually happens is the idea behind the[volatility risk premium](https://algotest.in/feature/vrp-analysis) . In this expiry, options priced in about 1,206 points and Sensex moved about 804.

## Sensex Straddle Chart: Track the Combined Premium


A straddle chart plots the ATM call plus the ATM put as one line. It shows the priced-in move shrinking or growing through the day.


On the Sensex option chain, open the Charts tab and choose Combined. It plots the combined premium of the legs you added, so a long straddle shows the full CE + PE cost moving minute by minute. Bought legs appear as negative values because you pay the premium.


Combined on the Sensex option chain. One call leg is shown here. Add the ATM put to plot the full straddle.

## Common Mistakes When Reading the Straddle


-


Using a strike far from the Sensex level adds intrinsic value to one leg and overstates the priced-in move.


-


Halving the straddle for each side places the breakevens too close to the strike.


-


Leaving out the time stamp makes the number impossible to compare with later readings.


-


Treating breakevens as intraday stop levels confuses an expiry outcome with a live price.


-


Matching an option price from one minute with a Sensex value from another can distort the breakevens on a fast-moving day.


## Turn the Expected Move Into a Rule You Can Test


The ATM straddle gives you one number for how far Sensex must travel before expiry. To trade it, fix when you read it, which side you take, where you exit and how much you risk per lot. Then check that rule across many past expiries, not just one week like this.

### FAQs


#### What is the ATM straddle price?


The ATM straddle price is the ATM call premium plus the ATM put premium for the same strike and expiry. On a Sensex option chain, read the Call LTP and Put LTP on the ATM row and add them.


#### What is the current straddle price of Sensex or Nifty?


It changes every minute, so you need a live chain to read it. Open the Sensex or[Nifty option chain](https://algotest.in/nifty-option-chain) , pick the expiry and add the ATM Call LTP and Put LTP.


#### How do you calculate Sensex straddle breakevens?


Add the straddle premium to the strike for the upper breakeven, and subtract it for the lower one. For the 81,100 straddle at 1,206.25 points, that gave 82,306.25 and 79,893.75.


#### What is the success rate of the long straddle strategy?


There is no fixed success rate. A long straddle wins at expiry only when the real move beats the priced-in move, which did not happen in this example. To get a number for your own entry and exit rules,[backtest them](https://algotest.in/feature/backtest) across past Sensex expiries.


#### Which is the best straddle strategy?


No single straddle strategy is best. A long straddle fits a view that Sensex will move more than the straddle prices in. A short straddle fits a view that it will move less, and needs strict loss limits and enough margin.


#### Can a straddle buyer lose money even when Sensex moves a lot?


Yes. In this example Sensex rose 804 points by expiry, and the buyer still lost 395.24 points per unit. The move fell short of the 1,206.25 points paid.
